q: What does IAM stand for in AWS?

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM does not stand for Internet Access Management.
exp.b: Correct. IAM stands for Identity and Access Management, which is used to manage access to AWS services and resources securely.
exp.c: Incorrect. IAM does not stand for Internal Account Management.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM does not stand for Integrated Authorization Module.

q: What is the default level of access a newly created IAM user has?

opts.a: Full access to all AWS services
opts.b: Read-only access to all AWS services
opts.c: No access to any AWS services
opts.d: Access only to the AWS Management Console

exp.a: Incorrect. A new IAM user has no permissions by default.
exp.b: Incorrect. Read-only access is not granted by default.
exp.c: Correct. By default, a newly created IAM user has no permissions. You must explicitly grant permissions.
exp.d: Incorrect. Console access must be explicitly enabled for a new user.

q: How many IAM users can you create per AWS account by default?

exp.a: Incorrect. The default limit is not 1000.
exp.b: Correct. The default limit is 5000 IAM users per AWS account.
exp.c: Incorrect. The default limit is not 10000.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is a limit on the number of IAM users.

q: How many IAM groups can an IAM user belong to at maximum?

exp.a: Incorrect. A user can belong to more than 5 groups.
exp.b: Correct. An IAM user can be a member of a maximum of 10 IAM groups.
exp.c: Incorrect. The maximum is not 15.
exp.d: Incorrect. The maximum is not 20.

q: What is the maximum number of IAM groups you can create per AWS account?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 100.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is not 200.
exp.c: Correct. You can create a maximum of 300 IAM groups per AWS account.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is not 500.

q: What is the maximum number of managed policies that can be attached to an IAM user?

exp.a: Incorrect. You can attach more than 5 managed policies.
exp.b: Correct. A maximum of 10 managed policies can be attached directly to an IAM user.
exp.c: Incorrect. The limit is not 15.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is not 20.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of an IAM policy?

exp.a: Incorrect. Effect (Allow/Deny) is a valid component of an IAM policy.
exp.b: Incorrect. Action specifies what actions are allowed or denied.
exp.c: Incorrect. Resource specifies which AWS resources the policy applies to.
exp.d: Correct. Duration is not a standard component of an IAM policy. The main elements are Version, Statement, Effect, Action, Resource, and optionally Condition.

q: What are the two types of access that can be configured for an IAM user?

opts.b: Programmatic access and AWS Management Console access

exp.a: Incorrect. CLI access falls under programmatic access.
exp.b: Correct. IAM users can be granted programmatic access (Access Key ID and Secret Access Key) and/or AWS Management Console access (username and password).
exp.c: Incorrect. Root and Admin are not types of access configurations.
exp.d: Incorrect. API and SDK access both fall under programmatic access.

q: What is the maximum size of an IAM managed policy?

exp.a: Incorrect. 2 KB is the limit for inline policies attached to a user.
exp.b: Incorrect. 5 KB is not the correct limit.
exp.c: Correct. The maximum size of a managed policy is 6,144 characters (not including whitespace).
exp.d: Incorrect. 10,240 characters is the limit for inline policies attached to a role.

q: Which IAM entity cannot be added to an IAM group?

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM users can be added to groups.
exp.b: Correct. IAM groups cannot contain other groups. Groups can only contain users.
exp.c: Incorrect. Users can be added to groups.
exp.d: Incorrect. Groups cannot be nested within other groups.

q: What is the format of an IAM policy document?

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM policies are not written in XML.
exp.b: Incorrect. IAM policies are not written in YAML (though CloudFormation templates can be).
exp.c: Correct. IAM policy documents are written in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation).
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM policies are not written in CSV.

q: What is an IAM Role?

opts.a: A permanent set of credentials for a user
opts.b: An identity with permission policies that determine what it can do, intended to be assumable
opts.c: A group of users with the same permissions

exp.a: Incorrect. Roles do not have permanent credentials; they provide temporary security credentials.
exp.b: Correct. An IAM role is an identity with permission policies that can be assumed by users, applications, or AWS services to gain temporary credentials.
exp.c: Incorrect. That describes an IAM group.
exp.d: Incorrect. MFA is a separate security feature.

q: How many access keys can an IAM user have at maximum?

exp.a: Incorrect. A user can have more than 1 access key.
exp.b: Correct. An IAM user can have a maximum of 2 access keys at a time. This allows for key rotation.
exp.c: Incorrect. The maximum is not 3.
exp.d: Incorrect. The maximum is not 5.

q: What happens when an explicit Deny and an explicit Allow conflict in IAM policies?

opts.c: The most recent policy takes precedence

exp.a: Incorrect. Allow does not take precedence over Deny.
exp.b: Correct. In IAM policy evaluation, an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow. This is a fundamental principle of IAM.
exp.c: Incorrect. The order of creation does not matter.
exp.d: Incorrect. No error is thrown; Deny simply wins.

q: Which of the following is a best practice for the AWS root account?

opts.a: Use it for daily administrative tasks
opts.b: Share its credentials with trusted administrators
opts.c: Enable MFA and avoid using it for everyday tasks
opts.d: Delete it after creating IAM users

exp.a: Incorrect. The root account should not be used for daily tasks.
exp.b: Incorrect. Root account credentials should never be shared.
exp.c: Correct. AWS best practice is to enable MFA on the root account, lock it away, and use IAM users for daily operations.
exp.d: Incorrect. The root account cannot be deleted.

q: What is the AWS Security Token Service (STS) used for?

exp.a: Incorrect. STS does not create permanent users.
exp.b: Correct. AWS STS provides temporary, limited-privilege security credentials for IAM users or federated users.
exp.c: Incorrect. S3 bucket policies are managed through S3.
exp.d: Incorrect. Encryption is handled by KMS and other services.

q: What is the default duration of temporary credentials issued by STS AssumeRole?

exp.a: Incorrect. 15 minutes is the minimum duration, not the default.
exp.b: Correct. The default duration for temporary credentials from AssumeRole is 1 hour (3600 seconds).
exp.c: Incorrect. 12 hours is the maximum duration for AssumeRole.
exp.d: Incorrect. 24 hours is not the default.

q: What is the maximum session duration for an IAM role (AssumeRole)?

exp.a: Incorrect. 1 hour is the default, not the maximum.
exp.b: Incorrect. 6 hours is not the maximum.
exp.c: Correct. The maximum session duration for an IAM role can be set up to 12 hours (43200 seconds).
exp.d: Incorrect. 36 hours exceeds the allowed maximum.

q: Which policy type is embedded directly in a single user, group, or role?

exp.a: Incorrect. Managed policies are standalone and can be attached to multiple entities.
exp.b: Correct. Inline policies are embedded directly in a single user, group, or role. They have a strict one-to-one relationship.
exp.c: Incorrect. Resource-based policies are attached to resources like S3 buckets.
exp.d: Incorrect. Service Control Policies are used in AWS Organizations.

q: What is the difference between AWS managed policies and customer managed policies?

opts.a: AWS managed policies can be edited; customer managed policies cannot
opts.b: Customer managed policies can be edited; AWS managed policies cannot
opts.d: AWS managed policies are free; customer managed policies cost extra

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS managed policies cannot be modified by customers.
exp.b: Correct. Customer managed policies are created and managed by you and can be edited. AWS managed policies are created and maintained by AWS and cannot be modified.
exp.c: Incorrect. There are significant differences between the two.
exp.d: Incorrect. Both are free to use; IAM is a free service.

q: Is IAM a global service or regional service?

opts.d: It is an Availability Zone-level service

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM is not region-specific.
exp.b: Correct. IAM is a global service. Users, groups, roles, and policies created in IAM are available across all AWS regions.
exp.c: Incorrect. IAM is always global regardless of configuration.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM is not tied to any specific Availability Zone.

q: What is the purpose of the IAM policy element 'Condition'?

opts.a: To specify the AWS account number
opts.b: To specify circumstances under which the policy grants or denies permission

exp.a: Incorrect. Account number is not specified through Condition.
exp.b: Correct. The Condition element allows you to specify conditions for when a policy is in effect, such as IP address restrictions, time-based conditions, or MFA requirements.
exp.c: Incorrect. Policy version is defined by the Version element.
exp.d: Incorrect. Condition does not list users.

q: What does the IAM policy element 'Principal' specify?

opts.a: The actions that are allowed or denied
opts.b: The resources affected by the policy
opts.c: The entity (user, account, service, or role) that is allowed or denied access

exp.a: Incorrect. Actions are specified by the Action element.
exp.b: Incorrect. Resources are specified by the Resource element.
exp.c: Correct. The Principal element specifies the entity (user, account, service, or role) that is allowed or denied access to a resource. It is used in resource-based policies.
exp.d: Incorrect. The effect is specified by the Effect element.

q: What is an IAM instance profile?

opts.a: A container for an IAM role that can be attached to an EC2 instance

exp.a: Correct. An instance profile is a container for an IAM role that you can use to pass role information to an EC2 instance when it starts.
exp.b: Incorrect. Instance profiles are not user accounts.
exp.c: Incorrect. Security groups are a separate networking concept.
exp.d: Incorrect. Instance profiles are not policies.

q: How many IAM roles can you create per AWS account by default?

exp.a: Incorrect. The default limit is not 250.
exp.b: Incorrect. The default limit is not 500.
exp.c: Correct. The default limit is 1000 IAM roles per AWS account.
exp.d: Incorrect. 5000 is the limit for IAM users, not roles.

q: What is the purpose of the IAM Access Analyzer?

opts.b: To identify resources shared with an external entity and analyze access

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM Access Analyzer does not create users.
exp.b: Correct. IAM Access Analyzer helps identify resources in your organization and accounts that are shared with an external entity, helping you identify unintended access.
exp.c: Incorrect. Encryption is not the purpose of Access Analyzer.
exp.d: Incorrect. Billing is managed by AWS Billing service.

q: What is the ARN format for an IAM user?

exp.a: Correct. The ARN format for an IAM user is arn:aws:iam::account-id:user/user-name. IAM is global, so the region field is empty.
exp.b: Incorrect. IAM ARNs do not include a region because IAM is a global service.
exp.c: Incorrect. This format is for roles, not users.
exp.d: Incorrect. This is an S3 ARN format.

q: What does MFA stand for in the context of IAM?

exp.a: Incorrect. MFA does not stand for Multiple Factor Access.
exp.b: Correct. MFA stands for Multi-Factor Authentication, which adds an extra layer of security by requiring a second form of verification.
exp.c: Incorrect. MFA has nothing to do with firewalls.
exp.d: Incorrect. MFA does not stand for Multi-Feature Authorization.

q: Which of the following MFA devices are supported by AWS IAM?

opts.a: Virtual MFA device, U2F security key, and hardware MFA device

exp.a: Correct. AWS supports virtual MFA devices (like Google Authenticator), U2F security keys (like YubiKey), and hardware MFA devices.
exp.b: Incorrect. AWS supports multiple types of MFA devices.
exp.c: Incorrect. Hardware MFA is one of several supported options.
exp.d: Incorrect. Biometric scanners are not directly supported as MFA by AWS IAM.

q: How many MFA devices can be assigned to a single IAM user?

exp.a: Incorrect. Users can have more than 1 MFA device.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit was increased beyond 2.
exp.c: Incorrect. The limit is not 5.
exp.d: Correct. As of recent updates, you can assign up to 8 MFA devices per IAM user.

q: What is the purpose of IAM credential reports?

opts.b: To list all IAM users and the status of their various credentials

exp.a: Incorrect. Credential reports are not related to billing.
exp.b: Correct. IAM credential reports list all users in your account and the status of their credentials including passwords, access keys, and MFA devices.
exp.c: Incorrect. Credential reports do not create users.
exp.d: Incorrect. EC2 monitoring is done through CloudWatch.

q: How often can you generate an IAM credential report?

opts.d: A new report can be generated once every 4 hours; cached report available anytime

exp.a: Correct. A new credential report can be generated once every 4 hours. Within that window, the cached version is returned.
exp.b: Incorrect. The interval is not 1 hour.
exp.c: Incorrect. The interval is not 24 hours.
exp.d: Incorrect. While the caching detail is partially correct, the standard answer is once every 4 hours.

q: What is the IAM policy evaluation logic order?

opts.b: Default Deny → Explicit Allow → Explicit Deny
opts.c: Explicit Deny → Organizations SCP → Resource-based → Identity-based → Permissions boundary → Default Deny
opts.d: All statements are evaluated; explicit Deny overrides any Allow; if no explicit Allow, default Deny applies

exp.a: Incorrect. This is not the correct evaluation order.
exp.b: Incorrect. This oversimplifies the process.
exp.c: Incorrect. While these elements are involved, this doesn't accurately represent the logic.
exp.d: Correct. AWS evaluates all applicable policies. By default, all requests are denied (implicit deny). An explicit Allow overrides the default deny. An explicit Deny always overrides any Allow.

q: What is a permissions boundary in IAM?

opts.a: The maximum permissions a user or role can have, regardless of identity-based policies

exp.a: Correct. A permissions boundary is an advanced feature that sets the maximum permissions that an identity-based policy can grant to an IAM entity. It does not grant permissions on its own.
exp.b: Incorrect. Permissions boundaries are not firewall rules.
exp.c: Incorrect. VPC configurations are unrelated to permissions boundaries.
exp.d: Incorrect. Permissions boundaries are not about encryption.

q: Which AWS service is used to enable Single Sign-On (SSO) for multiple AWS accounts?

opts.b: AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO)

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM alone does not provide SSO across multiple accounts.
exp.b: Correct. AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) provides centralized SSO access to multiple AWS accounts and business applications.
exp.c: Incorrect. Cognito is for application-level identity management.
exp.d: Incorrect. Direct Connect is a networking service.

q: What is federation in IAM?

opts.b: Allowing external identities (outside AWS) to access AWS resources without creating IAM users

exp.a: Incorrect. Federation is not about creating AWS accounts.
exp.b: Correct. Federation allows users from external identity providers (like Active Directory, SAML, or OIDC) to access AWS resources without needing separate IAM users.
exp.c: Incorrect. VPC peering connects VPCs.
exp.d: Incorrect. Replication is not related to federation.

q: What protocol does AWS IAM support for identity federation with enterprise identity providers?

exp.a: Incorrect. While OAuth/OIDC is supported for web identity federation, SAML 2.0 is the standard for enterprise federation.
exp.b: Correct. AWS IAM supports SAML 2.0 (Security Assertion Markup Language) for federating enterprise identity providers like Active Directory.
exp.c: Incorrect. LDAP is not directly used by IAM for federation.
exp.d: Incorrect. Kerberos is not directly supported by IAM for federation.

q: What is the maximum number of customer managed policies you can create per AWS account?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 1000.
exp.b: Correct. The default limit for customer managed policies per AWS account is 1500.
exp.c: Incorrect. The limit is not 5000.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is not 10000.

q: How many versions of a customer managed policy can you store?

exp.a: Incorrect. You can store more than 3 versions.
exp.b: Correct. You can store up to 5 versions of a customer managed policy. This allows you to roll back to a previous version if needed.
exp.c: Incorrect. The limit is not 10.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is a limit of 5 versions.

q: What is the purpose of the IAM policy element 'Resource'?

opts.a: To specify which AWS resource the policy applies to
opts.b: To specify who can access the policy
opts.c: To define the effect of the policy

exp.a: Correct. The Resource element specifies the object or objects that the statement covers, identified by their ARN.
exp.b: Incorrect. That is the function of the Principal element.
exp.c: Incorrect. That is the function of the Effect element.
exp.d: Incorrect. That is the function of the Version element.

q: What does the wildcard '*' mean in an IAM policy Action element?

exp.a: Incorrect. The wildcard means all, not none.
exp.b: Correct. The wildcard '*' in the Action element means all actions. For example, 's3:*' means all S3 actions.
exp.c: Incorrect. The wildcard does not distinguish between read and write.
exp.d: Incorrect. The wildcard includes all types of actions.

q: Which IAM feature allows you to require MFA for specific API actions?

exp.a: Incorrect. Groups alone cannot enforce MFA for specific actions.
exp.b: Correct. You can use the Condition element in a policy with the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition key to require MFA for specific API actions.
exp.c: Incorrect. Roles alone do not require MFA.
exp.d: Incorrect. Access keys are credentials, not MFA enforcement mechanisms.

q: What is a trust policy in IAM?

opts.a: A policy that defines what resources a role can access
opts.b: A policy that defines which entities can assume a role

exp.a: Incorrect. That describes a permissions policy.
exp.b: Correct. A trust policy (also called a role trust policy) is a JSON document that defines which principals (users, roles, accounts, or services) are allowed to assume the role.
exp.c: Incorrect. Trust policies are not related to encryption.
exp.d: Incorrect. Trust policies are not related to billing.

q: What is the maximum length of an IAM user name?

exp.a: Incorrect. The maximum is longer than 32 characters.
exp.b: Correct. IAM user names can be up to 64 characters long.
exp.c: Incorrect. 128 characters is the limit for role names and paths.
exp.d: Incorrect. 256 characters is not the correct limit.

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid IAM policy type?

exp.a: Incorrect. Identity-based policies are attached to users, groups, or roles.
exp.b: Incorrect. Resource-based policies are attached to resources like S3 buckets.
exp.c: Correct. Network-based policy is not a valid IAM policy type. The valid types include identity-based, resource-based, permissions boundaries, Organizations SCPs, ACLs, and session policies.
exp.d: Incorrect. SCPs are valid policy types used in AWS Organizations.

q: What AWS service allows you to set policies at the organization level to restrict member accounts?

opts.b: AWS Organizations with Service Control Policies (SCPs)

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM policies work at the account level, not organization level.
exp.b: Correct. AWS Organizations uses Service Control Policies (SCPs) to set permission guardrails across member accounts in an organization.
exp.c: Incorrect. Inspector is for vulnerability assessment.
exp.d: Incorrect. AWS Config is for compliance auditing.

q: What is the IAM Access Advisor feature used for?

opts.b: To show the services permissions granted to a user and when those services were last accessed

exp.a: Incorrect. Access Advisor does not create policies.
exp.b: Correct. IAM Access Advisor shows the service permissions granted to a user/role and when those services were last accessed. This helps you refine permissions based on actual usage.
exp.c: Incorrect. Access Advisor is not related to billing.
exp.d: Incorrect. Access Advisor is not related to VPN.

q: Can an IAM role be assumed by an IAM user from a different AWS account?

opts.a: No, roles can only be assumed within the same account
opts.b: Yes, through cross-account access using role trust policies
opts.c: Only if both accounts are in the same region

exp.a: Incorrect. Cross-account role assumption is a key feature of IAM.
exp.b: Correct. IAM roles can be assumed by users from other AWS accounts if the trust policy allows it. This is called cross-account access.
exp.c: Incorrect. IAM is global; region does not matter for role assumption.
exp.d: Incorrect. Any authorized IAM user can assume a role; root is not required.

q: What is the minimum password length that can be set in an IAM password policy?

exp.a: Incorrect. The minimum is not 1 character.
exp.b: Correct. The minimum password length in IAM password policy can be set as low as 6 characters (though best practice is much higher).
exp.c: Incorrect. 8 is the default but not the absolute minimum.
exp.d: Incorrect. 14 characters is a best practice but not the minimum allowed.

q: What is the maximum password length allowed in IAM?

exp.a: Incorrect. The maximum is not 64 characters.
exp.b: Correct. The maximum password length for IAM users is 128 characters.
exp.c: Incorrect. The maximum is not 256 characters.
exp.d: Incorrect. The maximum is not 512 characters.

q: Which IAM entity is used to delegate access to AWS services like EC2 or Lambda?

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM users are for human identities, not service delegation.
exp.b: Incorrect. Groups organize users; they don't delegate access to services.
exp.c: Correct. IAM roles are used to delegate access to AWS services. For example, an EC2 instance assumes a role to access S3.
exp.d: Incorrect. Policies define permissions but don't delegate access on their own.

q: What is the effect of attaching the AWS managed policy 'AdministratorAccess' to a user?

opts.a: The user can only read AWS resources
opts.b: The user gets full access to all AWS services and resources
opts.c: The user can only manage IAM
opts.d: The user gets access only to EC2

exp.a: Incorrect. AdministratorAccess provides full access, not read-only.
exp.b: Correct. The AdministratorAccess policy grants full access to all AWS services and resources, equivalent to Action: '*' on Resource: '*'.
exp.c: Incorrect. AdministratorAccess is not limited to IAM.
exp.d: Incorrect. The policy covers all services, not just EC2.

q: What is the purpose of the 'NotAction' element in an IAM policy?

opts.b: It matches every action except the specified actions

exp.a: Incorrect. NotAction does not deny all actions.
exp.b: Correct. NotAction explicitly matches everything EXCEPT the specified list of actions. It is useful for creating exceptions.
exp.c: Incorrect. NotAction does not specifically refer to read actions.
exp.d: Incorrect. NotAction does not disable the policy.

q: What happens to inline policies when the IAM entity (user/group/role) they are attached to is deleted?

opts.a: They are moved to another entity
opts.b: They are converted to managed policies
opts.d: They remain orphaned in the account

exp.a: Incorrect. Inline policies are not transferred.
exp.b: Incorrect. They are not automatically converted.
exp.c: Correct. Inline policies are embedded in the entity and are deleted when the entity is deleted. They have a one-to-one relationship.
exp.d: Incorrect. Inline policies do not become orphaned; they are deleted with the entity.

q: Which API call is used to assume an IAM role?

exp.a: Incorrect. GetSessionToken is used for MFA-protected API access, not role assumption.
exp.b: Correct. The sts:AssumeRole API call is used to assume an IAM role and obtain temporary security credentials.
exp.c: Incorrect. CreateRole creates a new role; it doesn't assume one.
exp.d: Incorrect. AttachRolePolicy attaches a policy to a role.

q: What is the purpose of the 'aws:SourceIp' condition key in an IAM policy?

opts.a: To specify the destination IP address
opts.b: To restrict access based on the requester's IP address
opts.c: To set up a VPN connection

exp.a: Incorrect. aws:SourceIp refers to the source, not destination.
exp.b: Correct. The aws:SourceIp condition key allows you to restrict access based on the IP address from which the request originates.
exp.c: Incorrect. VPN is configured through other services.
exp.d: Incorrect. DNS is managed by Route 53.

q: What is the IAM policy simulator used for?

opts.b: To test and troubleshoot IAM policies without actually making API calls

exp.a: Incorrect. The simulator does not create policies.
exp.b: Correct. The IAM Policy Simulator allows you to test the effects of IAM policies before committing them, helping you understand which actions are allowed or denied.
exp.c: Incorrect. The simulator has nothing to do with encryption.
exp.d: Incorrect. CPU monitoring is done through CloudWatch.

q: What is the maximum number of managed policies that can be attached to an IAM role?

exp.a: Incorrect. You can attach more than 5.
exp.b: Correct. A maximum of 10 managed policies can be attached to a single IAM role.
exp.c: Incorrect. The limit is not 15.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is not 20.

q: What is the maximum number of managed policies that can be attached to an IAM group?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 5.
exp.b: Correct. A maximum of 10 managed policies can be attached to a single IAM group.
exp.c: Incorrect. The limit is not 15.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is not 20.

q: What does the IAM tag feature allow you to do?

opts.b: Add metadata to IAM resources for organization and access control

exp.a: Incorrect. Tags do not delete users.
exp.b: Correct. IAM tags allow you to add key-value pairs as metadata to IAM resources (users, roles, policies). Tags can also be used in policy conditions for attribute-based access control (ABAC).
exp.c: Incorrect. VPCs are not created through IAM tags.
exp.d: Incorrect. Auto-scaling is a separate service.

q: What is the maximum number of tags you can attach to an IAM user or role?

exp.a: Incorrect. You can attach more than 10 tags.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is not 25.
exp.c: Correct. You can attach a maximum of 50 tags to an IAM user or role.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is not 100.

q: What is the 'Effect' element in an IAM policy?

opts.b: It specifies whether the statement allows or denies access

exp.a: Incorrect. Region is not specified by the Effect element.
exp.b: Correct. The Effect element specifies whether the policy statement results in an Allow or a Deny. These are the only two valid values.
exp.c: Incorrect. The Resource element specifies ARNs.
exp.d: Incorrect. The Version element specifies the policy version.

q: Which of the following is true about the root user in AWS?

opts.a: It can be restricted by IAM policies
opts.b: It has unrestricted access to all resources and cannot be limited by IAM policies

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM policies cannot restrict the root user (though SCPs can limit it in member accounts).
exp.b: Correct. The root user has complete, unrestricted access to all resources in the AWS account. IAM policies cannot be applied to restrict it.
exp.c: Incorrect. The root user cannot be deleted.
exp.d: Incorrect. MFA can and should be enabled on the root user.

q: What is the cost of using AWS IAM?

opts.d: Included in AWS Support plan costs

exp.a: Incorrect. There is no per-user charge.
exp.b: Incorrect. There is no per-policy charge.
exp.c: Correct. AWS IAM is offered at no additional charge. You are only charged for the AWS services your users access.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM is free regardless of your support plan.

q: What is an IAM policy's 'Statement' element?

opts.b: The main element of a policy containing individual permission rules
opts.d: The creation date of the policy

exp.a: Incorrect. The policy name is separate from the Statement.
exp.b: Correct. The Statement element is the main element of a policy. It contains an array of individual statements, each of which includes Effect, Action, Resource, and optionally Condition and Principal.
exp.c: Incorrect. The ARN is a unique identifier for the policy.
exp.d: Incorrect. The creation date is metadata, not part of the Statement.
